paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student model using a teacher’s probabilities over classes instead of labels that put all their weight on one class. This paper asks why that replacement can help, and why a teacher with higher classification accuracy does not necessarily produce a better student. It approaches these questions through the statistics of the student’s training objective.

The central observation concerns an ideal teacher that supplies the true class probabilities. Such a teacher can reduce the variance of the objective the student learns from, which can improve performance. Real teachers only approximate those probabilities, so the authors establish a bias–variance tradeoff describing the value of these imperfect estimates.

This analysis makes probability estimation quality a formal criterion for choosing a useful teacher. Getting the winning class right does not by itself capture how helpful the full probability distribution will be for learning. The paper also illustrates how this perspective supports applications of distillation to bipartite ranking and multiclass retrieval, extending the statistical argument beyond ordinary classification.
icml-2021-a-statistical-perspective-on-d.tldr: Distillation can help by reducing training-objective variance, with teacher probability quality governing a bias–variance tradeoff.

paragraphs: Learning performance depends on how a model and its loss interact with the input distribution and the function being learned. This paper examines that interaction through high-dimensional ridge regression. Keeping the model relatively simple lets the analysis focus on arbitrary correlations between input features and the target function, rather than assuming these ingredients are unrelated.

The authors find that substantially fewer examples can be needed when the target function aligns with anisotropy in the data: the fact that the input distribution has different structure in different directions. This makes the relationship between the data and the target central to sample complexity, rather than treating the amount of data as the only relevant statistical ingredient.

The theory also produces multiple descent curves and a sequence of phase transitions as the amount of data changes. These transitions affect prediction performance, the loss landscape, and the best regularization choice. Together, they explain the reported sample-complexity reductions and repeated descent behavior within the ridge-regression analysis.
icml-2021-a-theory-of-high-dimensional-r.tldr: High-dimensional ridge-regression theory shows how input–target alignment can reduce sample needs and produce multiple descent curves.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to identify the best policy in a discounted Markov decision process using as few samples as possible. The learner has access to a generative model that supplies samples of the environment. The central decision is how to allocate sampling effort so that the best policy can be identified quickly.

The authors first derive a lower bound on the samples any learning algorithm requires for the particular problem. Its optimal allocation is described by a non-convex optimization problem, making it difficult to use directly. They then derive a simple, tight upper bound on that lower bound, yielding an explicit allocation that is nearly optimal.

The allocation reflects properties such as the gaps between optimal and suboptimal choices and the variance of next-state values. Consequently, it responds to the difficulty of the specific environment. Their KLB-TS algorithm tracks this allocation, with asymptotic sample-complexity guarantees both almost surely and in expectation. Numerical comparisons illustrate its advantages against existing algorithms.
icml-2021-adaptive-sampling-for-best-pol.tldr: KLB-TS adaptively tracks an explicit, nearly optimal sampling allocation to identify the best policy efficiently.

paragraphs: This paper addresses multiclass classification when only a very small labeled dataset is available, but several weak supervision sources provide additional information. Those sources may be arbitrarily correlated, so the approach does not depend on treating their outputs as independent evidence. The task is to turn imperfect supervision into a learning problem with performance guarantees.

The method rigorously estimates statistics of the supervision sources and uses them to constrain possible labelings of unlabeled examples. Training then considers an adversarial choice among the labelings that satisfy those constraints. The authors prove that their algorithm converges to a model minimizing empirical risk under this adversarial formulation.

The theoretical guarantees depend on the information supplied by the weak sources, connecting the strength of the result to the available supervision. Sources also need not use the same label space as the final classification task, allowing information expressed through different categories to contribute. Experiments on multiple image-classification tasks demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness.
icml-2021-adversarial-multi-class-learni.tldr: An adversarial learning formulation combines correlated weak supervision sources with guarantees tied to the information they provide.

paragraphs: Structured prediction often requires outputs to satisfy rules, such as consistency among labels in a hierarchy. These constraints help exclude infeasible answers, but they are commonly written by hand. This paper asks whether the rules themselves can be learned from examples, so that a system can recover the structure governing acceptable outputs.

The authors formulate prediction as an integer linear programming problem. Given objective-function coefficients and their corresponding solutions, the method estimates inner and outer polytopes of the feasible set. These geometric approximations support the discovery of constraints describing which solutions are allowed. The paper also analyzes the tightness of the approximations and the reliability of the resulting constraints.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world applications show that the approach can identify feasible sets at scale. It learns to solve 9×9 Sudoku and minimum spanning tree problems from examples without receiving their underlying rules. It can also work with a neural network to learn hierarchical label structure in multilabel classification.
icml-2021-an-integer-linear-programming-.tldr: The framework learns structured-output constraints from optimization examples by estimating the geometry of feasible solutions.

paragraphs: Many group-fairness methods protect demographic groups specified before training. This paper argues that such a setup cannot anticipate every group that may later face poor service. It studies fairness through worst-case risk across potential subgroups, without requiring predefined demographic categories at either training or test time.

The proposed Blind Pareto Fairness method uses no-regret dynamics to recover a fair minimax classifier. Its objective reduces the worst-case risk of any potential subgroup meeting a sufficient-size requirement. At the same time, it guarantees the best possible service for the remaining population within the proposed fairness formulation. This connects protection for poorly served groups with the treatment of everyone else.

The subgroup-size qualification is part of the stated protection: the method’s claim concerns groups of sufficient size. Experiments on multiple standard datasets show improved worst-case risk together with better service for the remaining population. These findings support the usefulness of examining fairness beyond a fixed list of protected groups.
icml-2021-blind-pareto-fairness-and-subg.tldr: Blind Pareto Fairness protects sufficiently large potential subgroups while optimizing service for the remaining population.

paragraphs: When some nodes in a network have known attributes, the network’s connections may help estimate attributes for the others. This paper develops a way to measure similarity between nodes using the patterns in their two-hop neighborhoods. Its CN-VEC algorithm uses that similarity in a procedure resembling nearest-neighbor regression.

The authors prove consistency for a broad range of models when node degree grows faster than the cube root of the number of nodes, up to logarithmic factors. Under that condition, the estimator has the stated large-network guarantee. The approach therefore links the usefulness of local network patterns to a concrete requirement on network density.

For low-rank latent-variable models, the paper also examines estimating hidden node representations with singular value decomposition before performing nonparametric regression. That method is consistent under less demanding sparsity conditions. Nevertheless, experiments suggest that local CN-VEC can outperform or match the global SVD-RBF approach on low-rank models. Simulated and real-data comparisons further demonstrate the algorithms’ effectiveness against existing methods.
icml-2021-consistent-nonparametric-metho.tldr: Two-hop neighborhood similarity enables consistent estimation of missing node attributes under a stated network-density condition.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to influence a changing process on a network when only limited interventions are available. Examples include choosing people for virus testing, targeting marketing efforts, and inspecting posts for spreading misinformation. In these settings, decisions must be made while the process evolves and while its full state is only partly observed.

The authors formulate the task as a sequential decision problem over a temporal graph process. The title identifies reinforcement learning and graph neural networks as the tools used for control. The formulation brings together three difficulties: exponentially many possible states, combinations of intervention choices, and incomplete observations. The paper develops a tractable scheme for handling this setup.

The approach is successfully applied to prioritizing node tests to curb epidemic spread and to maximizing influence on a graph. These applications illustrate how the same framework can address different goals for network dynamics. The shared question is where to spend scarce interventions as the network process changes over time.
icml-2021-controlling-graph-dynamics-wit.tldr: A tractable sequential decision framework uses reinforcement learning and graph neural networks to control partially observed network processes.

paragraphs: A successful outcome in reinforcement learning may reflect a good action, favorable external events, or decisions taken later. Credit assignment asks how much influence the action itself had on future rewards. This paper adapts counterfactual reasoning from causality to help separate these contributions within model-free reinforcement learning.

The key idea is to learn useful information from a trajectory and condition value functions on future events. The authors build a family of policy-gradient algorithms that use these future-conditional value functions as baselines or critics. They prove low-variance properties for these algorithms, addressing the noise that can obscure an action’s contribution during learning.

Using hindsight introduces a potential source of bias if the future information reveals the action being evaluated. The method therefore constrains the hindsight information so that it contains no information about the agent’s actions. This restriction is central to the validity of the approach. Experiments on illustrative and challenging problems demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness and validity.
icml-2021-counterfactual-credit-assignme.tldr: Action-independent hindsight helps construct low-variance policy-gradient methods for separating an action’s contribution from luck.

paragraphs: EfficientTTS addresses the need to turn text into high-quality speech quickly while keeping training efficient. It is a non-autoregressive architecture with a stable, end-to-end procedure that optimizes all its parameters. The approach removes the need for external aligners used by the dominant non-autoregressive systems discussed in the paper.

Its central mechanism is a new approach to monotonic alignment: the correspondence between the text sequence and the speech sequence must follow an ordered progression. The authors impose these alignment constraints with almost no additional computation. Combining the mechanism with different feed-forward network structures produces a family of models for both text-to-melspectrogram and direct text-to-waveform generation.

Experiments report significant improvements over counterparts including Tacotron 2 and Glow-TTS in speech quality, training efficiency, and synthesis speed. The models also produce speech described as robust and diverse. The authors further demonstrate that the alignment approach can be extended to autoregressive systems such as Tacotron 2, broadening its use beyond the proposed non-autoregressive architecture.
icml-2021-efficienttts-an-efficient-and-.tldr: EfficientTTS learns monotonic text–speech alignment end to end, with reported gains in speech quality and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Some classification tasks require predictions to respect a known ordering: increasing an input feature, while holding other features fixed, must not decrease the prediction. Such monotonicity requirements constrain how a classifier behaves. This paper studies how that structure can support formal explanations of predictions, an area the authors describe as having few dedicated, broadly applicable methods.

The authors introduce algorithms for computing one formal explanation of a monotonic classifier treated as a black box. Because the algorithms work through the classifier’s behavior, the contribution is not tied to one particular model architecture. Their computational complexity is polynomial, and specifically linear in the classifier’s runtime complexity, giving a concrete efficiency result for obtaining an explanation.

The paper also presents a practically efficient, model-agnostic algorithm for enumerating formal explanations. This addresses the separate task of finding multiple explanations rather than stopping after one. Together, the results make monotonicity useful not only as a constraint on predictions but also as structure that enables efficient explanation procedures.
icml-2021-explanations-for-monotonic-cla.tldr: Monotonicity enables efficient black-box algorithms for computing and enumerating formal classifier explanations.

paragraphs: An agent may initially need to explore an unknown environment without receiving rewards. This paper studies pure exploration, where the immediate goal is gathering useful knowledge. It examines exploration bonuses that encourage visits to unfamiliar state–action pairs and asks how their mathematical form affects learning speed.

A common bonus decreases as the inverse square root of a pair’s visit count. For reward-free exploration, the authors show that bonuses decreasing as the inverse of the count yield faster learning rates. Specifically, they improve known upper bounds in their dependence on the horizon, the length of the decision sequence. The result identifies a benefit of this faster-decaying bonus for the stated exploration objective.

The paper also studies best-policy identification, where rewards are observed but poor choices during exploration are not penalized. An improved analysis of when learning stops reduces the sample-complexity bound by a factor equal to the horizon. Both contributions sharpen guarantees for gathering enough information before committing to a policy.
icml-2021-fast-active-learning-for-pure-.tldr: Inverse-count bonuses improve reward-free exploration bounds, while sharper stopping-time analysis improves best-policy identification sample complexity.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can improve performance against an attacker while increasing error on ordinary data. This paper studies that tension when the attacker can change the test distribution within a Wasserstein-distance neighborhood of the training distribution. The neighborhood’s radius specifies how much power the attacker has to alter the distribution.

The authors derive Pareto-optimal tradeoffs between ordinary and adversarial risk: combinations where improving one risk cannot be achieved without worsening the other within the model class considered. Their analysis assumes infinitely much data while keeping feature dimension fixed. It covers linear regression, linear classification under a Gaussian-mixture data model, and regression with random features.

A tradeoff appears in all three settings. The random-features model also has an interpretation as a two-layer neural network with random first-layer weights. The paper characterizes how the tradeoff curves depend on factors including feature correlations, attacker strength, and network width. These results describe fundamental compromises in the analyzed settings even after finite-data uncertainty has been removed.
icml-2021-fundamental-tradeoffs-in-distr.tldr: The paper derives optimal ordinary-risk versus adversarial-risk tradeoffs for three model settings in an infinite-data regime.

paragraphs: Optimization becomes difficult when a non-convex surface contains many local minima. Finding good solutions can require many iterations or repeated random restarts. Learn2Hop approaches this problem by using meta-learning to learn an optimization algorithm across different loss landscapes, aiming to make the search for low-valued solutions more efficient.

The paper focuses on atomic structural optimization, where the objective is to find low-energy arrangements of many atoms. Its studied systems include bimetallic clusters and disordered silicon. In these problems, the authors find that the learned optimizer develops a hopping behavior that supports exploration of the landscape and increases the rate at which low-energy minima are discovered.

The learned optimizers also show promising generalization to tasks not encountered before, including new elements or compositions, with reported efficiency gains. The finding concerns improved exploration and discovery of low-energy configurations. It suggests that learning how to move across many-minima landscapes can transfer useful optimization behavior across the atomic problems examined.
icml-2021-learn2hop-learned-optimization.tldr: Learn2Hop learns hopping behavior that speeds discovery of low-energy atomic configurations and shows promising transfer to unseen tasks.

paragraphs: Multi-agent learning often concentrates on teams with shared rewards or on zero-sum competition. This paper studies a setting where agents pursue individual goals and states and actions can be continuous. It focuses on stochastic potential games, a structured class of nonzero-sum games that accommodates these different agent objectives.

The authors introduce a learning method and prove that independent agents can learn Nash-equilibrium strategies in polynomial time for the studied setting. A Nash equilibrium describes strategies for which no individual agent benefits from changing its own strategy alone. The theoretical result connects this equilibrium objective to efficient learning in the stochastic-potential-game class.

The framework is demonstrated on Coordination Navigation and large selfish routing games, tasks the authors characterize as previously unsolved in this context. It also outperforms the named multi-agent baselines MADDPG and COMIX in those scenarios. These findings support extending multi-agent reinforcement learning to individual incentives and continuous environments when the game has the potential structure analyzed in the paper.
icml-2021-learning-in-nonzero-sum-stocha.tldr: A learning method achieves polynomial-time Nash-equilibrium learning in continuous stochastic potential games and improves results on studied tasks.

paragraphs: Classical convergence analyses often describe an objective using uniform conditions on its smoothness and the relationship between gradients and optimality. This paper introduces non-uniform refinements of smoothness and the Łojasiewicz inequality, motivated by machine-learning objectives. These definitions describe geometry that can vary across the objective landscape.

The refinements motivate geometry-aware first-order methods with global convergence faster than the classical inverse-square iteration lower bounds referenced in the paper. For policy-gradient optimization, the authors show that normalizing gradient ascent can yield exponential convergence in the iteration count, with less overhead than existing algorithms. Their analysis makes the objective’s non-uniform structure central to this acceleration.

For generalized linear model training, a geometry-aware normalized gradient-descent method also achieves linear convergence, improving the best known results cited by the authors. The proposed methods additionally escape plateaus faster than standard gradient descent. Experiments illustrate and complement these theoretical findings. The accelerated guarantees concern the analyzed geometry and problems, giving a structured route to faster non-convex optimization.
icml-2021-leveraging-non-uniformity-in-f.tldr: Non-uniform geometric conditions motivate normalized gradient methods with faster convergence for policy gradients and generalized linear models.

paragraphs: This paper views adversarial examples as a zero-sum game between an attacker and a classifier. The attacker seeks outcomes that harm classification, while the classifier seeks robustness. The central question is whether the game has mixed Nash equilibria, which allow players to randomize their strategies instead of committing to a single choice.

The authors show the necessity of considering randomization for both players, whereas earlier work usually allowed it for only one. They establish that the game has no duality gap: the two opposing optimization perspectives agree on its value. The stated consequence is that approximate Nash equilibria always exist, providing a theoretical target for robust learning.

The paper also supplies optimization algorithms that learn a mixture of classifiers approximately achieving the game’s value. This connects the equilibrium analysis to procedures for constructing an optimally robust randomized classifier in the studied formulation. The approximation qualification matters: the algorithms aim to approach the game value, and the existence result explicitly guarantees approximate equilibria.
icml-2021-mixed-nash-equilibria-in-the-a.tldr: Allowing both attacker and classifier to randomize yields approximate-equilibrium guarantees and algorithms for learning robust classifier mixtures.

paragraphs: Methods for two-player constant-sum games do not cover the full range of multi-agent interactions. This paper develops Joint Policy-Space Response Oracles, or JPSRO, for training agents in games with multiple players and general-sum rewards. It considers extensive-form games, where the interaction has a sequential decision structure.

The authors prove that JPSRO converges to an equilibrium and propose correlated equilibria as promising meta-solvers within the training framework. These meta-solvers address the strategic combinations used during training. Because selecting a correlated equilibrium is itself a problem, the paper introduces Maximum Gini Correlated Equilibrium as a principled and computationally efficient family of solutions for that selection task.

Experiments using correlated-equilibrium meta-solvers demonstrate convergence on games with multiple players and general-sum rewards. The contribution therefore combines a training algorithm, a convergence result, and a way to select among correlated-equilibrium solutions. Together, these components extend the equilibrium-based training approach to interactions beyond the well-studied two-player constant-sum setting.
icml-2021-multi-agent-training-beyond-ze.tldr: JPSRO extends equilibrium-convergent training to multiplayer general-sum games, using correlated-equilibrium selection methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in environments whose rewards and transition rules change over time. Changes may be arbitrary, provided their total accumulated variation stays within specified budgets. The authors propose RestartQ-UCB, a restarted Q-learning algorithm with upper confidence bounds, and describe it as the first model-free algorithm for non-stationary reinforcement learning.

The analysis measures dynamic regret, capturing performance loss against a benchmark that changes with the environment. With Freedman-type exploration bonuses, the regret bound scales as the two-thirds power of total time and the one-third power of the variation budget, alongside state, action, and horizon factors. An information-theoretic lower bound matches these principal dependencies, with a different horizon factor, supporting the near-optimality claim.

Numerical experiments validate advantages in cumulative rewards and computational efficiency. The authors also demonstrate relevance to multi-agent reinforcement learning, where changing behavior creates non-stationarity. The result connects a model-free learning procedure to quantitative guarantees that explicitly account for how much the environment changes.
icml-2021-near-optimal-model-free-reinfo.tldr: RestartQ-UCB achieves near-optimal dynamic-regret guarantees when rewards and transitions change within cumulative variation budgets.

paragraphs: This paper asks which observed time series are direct or indirect causes of an observed target series when some variables remain hidden. The presence of latent variables makes causal feature selection more demanding than simply finding predictive associations. The authors propose a constraint-based method that uses conditional-independence relationships to decide whether a candidate series is a cause.

Under specified graph constraints, the method is proved sound and complete. These guarantees mean that the causal selection procedure is correct and comprehensive within the graph setting covered by the theory. Both the theoretical procedure and the estimation algorithm require only two conditional-independence tests for each observed candidate time series.

The method also chooses its conditioning set in a way that improves the signal-to-noise ratio. This makes the choice of variables used in the tests part of the approach’s contribution. Applications to real data and a broad range of simulations yield very low false-positive rates and relatively low false-negative rates, supporting the method’s practical effectiveness.
icml-2021-necessary-and-sufficient-condi.tldr: Under graph constraints, two conditional-independence tests per candidate suffice for sound and complete causal time-series feature selection.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can be expensive because it commonly trains many candidate networks to judge their quality. This paper investigates whether an untrained network already contains a useful signal about its eventual trained accuracy. Such a signal could make it much cheaper to choose promising architectures during search.

The authors examine how activations overlap across data points in networks before training. They motivate a measure based on that overlap that is usefully indicative of trained performance. A simple search algorithm uses the measure to find powerful networks in seconds on a single GPU, without training the candidates during the search process.

The approach is evaluated on NAS-Bench-101, NAS-Bench-201, NATS-Bench, and Network Design Spaces. The authors also examine combining it with a more expensive method through an adaptation of regularized evolutionary search. The contribution is a fast architecture-selection signal that partially anticipates trained performance, making both standalone search and integration with existing search procedures possible.
icml-2021-neural-architecture-search-wit.tldr: Activation overlap in untrained networks provides a useful performance signal for architecture search in seconds on one GPU.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning uses expert behavior to recover a reward function representing a task. This paper studies that recovery with transfer in mind: the reward may later be used in a different environment. It analyzes the class of reward functions compatible with the expert’s behavior, making the set of plausible rewards an explicit theoretical object.

The authors examine how incomplete knowledge of the expert’s policy and the environment affects reward reconstruction. They then trace how reconstruction error carries through to the performance of a policy learned after transferring the reward. This links uncertainty during reward learning to the eventual consequences in the new environment.

Using these findings, the paper develops a provably efficient active-sampling approach that accounts for the need to transfer the reward. The sampling method can be paired with a wide variety of inverse-reinforcement-learning algorithms. Numerical simulations on benchmark environments accompany the theory, illustrating an approach in which information gathering is shaped by the reward’s intended use after transfer.
icml-2021-provably-efficient-learning-of.tldr: A transfer-aware analysis of reward-reconstruction error leads to provably efficient active sampling for inverse reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Estimating causal effects is difficult when hidden variables confound the relationship being studied. This paper considers a setting where the confounders are unobserved but proxy variables for them are available. Within proximal causal learning, it develops nonlinear estimation methods that can use those observed proxies.

The authors propose two kernel-based approaches: a two-stage regression method and a maximum moment restriction method. They provide a unified view of these approaches as ways to solve the underlying nonlinear problem. Their methods also apply to a broader class of inverse problems described by Fredholm integral equations, connecting the causal task to a general mathematical formulation.

Both algorithms receive consistency guarantees. Experiments on synthetic data and data simulating a real-world task show competitive performance, including improvements over earlier methods not suited to using proxy variables. The results support the value of incorporating proxies through these nonlinear estimators in the studied setting, where useful information about hidden confounding is available indirectly.
icml-2021-proximal-causal-learning-with-.tldr: Two consistent kernel-based methods estimate nonlinear causal effects using observed proxies for hidden confounders.

paragraphs: This paper develops a general approach to unsupervised learning when the observed data distribution has been perturbed. Its key assumption is that the perturbing distribution produces larger losses relative to the allowed class of models. This creates a basis for distinguishing the perturbation’s influence through the losses encountered during learning.

The proposed descent algorithm minimizes an L-statistic criterion that assigns greater weight to smaller losses. Under the stated assumption, this weighting reduces the influence associated with the perturbing distribution. The analysis measures robustness through bounds on reconstruction error relative to the original, unperturbed distribution, connecting the modified objective to the quality of the desired reconstruction.

The authors also prove uniform convergence bounds for the criterion across several popular unsupervised models. These results provide theoretical support for learning with the proposed loss weighting. Numerical experiments on k-means clustering and principal subspace analysis demonstrate effectiveness in the tested settings. The assumption linking perturbations to higher losses is central to the approach’s robustness argument.
icml-2021-robust-unsupervised-learning-v.tldr: Weighting smaller losses more heavily supports robust unsupervised learning when perturbing data produces larger losses.

paragraphs: UCB Momentum Q-learning, or UCBMQ, is designed for episodic reinforcement learning with tabular states and actions. The environment may depend on the stage within an episode. The algorithm combines Q-learning with a momentum term and optimistic estimates that encourage exploration when the agent remains uncertain.

The technical contribution is using momentum to correct Q-learning’s bias while controlling its contribution to the second-order regret term. The guarantee has a leading term proportional to the square root of H³SAT and an additional H⁴SA term, apart from logarithmic factors. Here H is episode length, S and A count states and actions, and T counts episodes.

For sufficiently many episodes, the leading term matches the stated lower-bound scaling up to logarithmic factors. At the same time, the additional term grows only linearly with the number of states. The authors identify UCBMQ as the first algorithm to achieve both properties together. This matters because the guarantee controls both long-run regret and the extra contribution associated with the state-space size.
icml-2021-ucb-momentum-q-learning-correc.tldr: UCBMQ uses momentum to correct Q-learning bias while combining near-optimal leading regret with a second-order term linear in state count.
